endorsements.title: Adoption of AI in Healthcare Delivery Systems: Early Applications and Impacts
endorsements.quote: Some Taskforce organizations even piloted vendors side-by-side.

endorsements.title: A Conceptual Model for Ambient AI Adoption: Perspectives From Academia and Industry
endorsements.quote: At the system level, the organization pilots both tools in a small number of clinical settings with different workflows and documentation norms.

evidence.title: A Randomized-Clinical Trial of Two Ambient Artificial Intelligence Scribes: Measuring Documentation Efficiency and Physician Burnout
evidence.outcome: Time-in-note change comparing two ambient scribe products head-to-head and versus control
evidence.effect: Nabla: -9.5% [-17.2,-1.8] vs control and -7.8% [-15.5,-0.1] vs DAX; DAX vs control -1.7% [-9.4,+5.9], p=.66. Burnout gains were similar across vendors.
evidence.quote: Nabla users experienced a 9.5% [95% CI:-17.2%,-1.8%] (p=.02) decrease in time-in-note versus the control group and a 7.8% [-15.5%,-0.1%] (p=.05) decrease versus DAX users, while DAX users exhibited no significant change versus control (-1.7% [-9.4%,+5.9%]; p=.66).

evidence.title: Comparing ambient scribes: a randomized crossover clinical trial addressing ambient scribe technologies' impact on physician burnout
evidence.venue: Journal of the American Medical Informatics Association : JAMIA
evidence.outcome: Clinician workflow satisfaction, burnout, and documentation time comparing two ambient scribe products in randomized crossover pilot
evidence.effect: Product B yielded greater satisfaction improvement (2.51 vs 1.91; mean difference 0.60, 95% CI 0.32-0.90) and greater reduction in minutes-in-notes (B - A = -3.19 minutes; 95% CI -4.87 to -1.50) than product A.
evidence.quote: Clinicians reported greater improvements in satisfaction with product B (2.51 points on a 7-point scale) compared to product A (1.91 points; mean difference: 0.60, 95% CI: 0.32-0.90).

evidence.title: Ambient Artificial Intelligence Versus Human Scribes in the Emergency Department
evidence.outcome: Side-by-side local pilot comparing AI scribe with human scribe on quality and EHR time
evidence.effect: AI scribes associated with more EHR notes time, more physician note contribution, and similar to lower quality notes versus human scribes.
evidence.quote: In comparison to human scribes, AI scribes were associated with more time spent in the electronic health record notes section, more physician note contribution, and similar to lower quality notes.

evidence.title: Crossover Evaluation of Two Ambient AI Scribe Tools in the Emergency Department
evidence.outcome: Clinician-perceived burden, usability, note quality, satisfaction and preference between two scribes in side-by-side local pilot
evidence.effect: DAX favored on unadjusted burden (median 1.5 vs 2, p=0.025), PDQI-9 (39 vs 36.5, p=0.011) and satisfaction (9 vs 7.5, p=0.015); usability equal (SUS 73.5 vs 73.5); adjusted models showed order effects, no overall preference.
evidence.quote: DAX received higher satisfaction ratings (median likelihood-to-recommend: 9 vs. 7.5; p = 0.015), but adjusted models suggested these differences reflected order effects more than inherent tool differences.
evidence.sample_unit: emergency department faculty physicians who completed both phases

evidence.title: Implementing Artificial Intelligence-Enabled Ambient Documentation Technology for Ambulatory Clinicians: An Innovation Evaluation
evidence.outcome: Utilization and user experience of two ambient scribe vendors compared in local pilot
evidence.effect: Vendor B showed higher utilization rates and superior user experience compared to Vendor A.
evidence.quote: "Vendor B" showed higher utilization rates and superior user experience compared to "Vendor A."

evidence.title: Selecting, Scaling, and Measuring the Value of Ambient AI in a Nonacademic Health System: Multiphase Pilot Study
evidence.outcome: Vendor selection through side-by-side simulation and workflow demonstrations of 4 ambient scribe vendors
evidence.effect: Multiphase comparison of 4 vendors, narrowed to 2 and then 1, reported to have minimized vendor influence and cognitive bias in selection; no comparative counterfactual outcome reported.
evidence.quote: Our structured, multiphase evaluation process minimized vendor influence and cognitive bias during selection, validated results through real-world clinical testing, and enabled a system-wide rollout.

evidence.title: Real-world multimetric comparison of four commercial artificial intelligence solutions for intracranial hemorrhage detection
evidence.outcome: Side-by-side local comparison of candidate AI products to inform selection
evidence.effect: Meaningful differences emerged among four products in confirmatory performance and volumetric agreement despite similar AUROC; no single solution universally optimal.
evidence.quote: The algorithm-specific performance trade-offs identified in this study suggest that no single AI solution is universally optimal

evidence.title: The value of simulation testing for the evaluation of ambient digital scribes: a case report
evidence.venue: Journal of the American Medical Informatics Association : JAMIA
evidence.outcome: Side-by-side comparison of two ambient scribe products on edit time, errors, and ratings
evidence.effect: Product A draft notes took significantly longer to edit, had fewer omissions, and more additions and irrelevant or misplaced text errors than Product B; Product A was rated as performing better for most encounters.
evidence.quote: Ambient Digital Scribe Product A draft notes took significantly longer to edit, had fewer omissions, and more additions and irrelevant or misplaced text errors than ADS Product B.

evidence.title: Comparative evaluation of ambient digital scribe systems in clinical documentation
evidence.venue: Journal of the American Medical Informatics Association : JAMIA
evidence.outcome: Side-by-side comparison of 3 ambient scribe vendors on identical recordings, Likert ratings and error audit
evidence.effect: Vendor A had highest Likert ratings (Friedman χ²(2)=15.529, P<.001 short visit); audit found fewest errors in Vendor B (n=3), then A (n=8), C (n=9). Vendor rankings differed by method.
evidence.quote: In this exploratory sample, Vendor A received the highest mean Likert ratings across all 4 domains (Friedman χ²(2) = 15.529, P < .001 short visit; χ²(2) = 10.753, P = .005 long visit).

evidence.title: Rapid Evaluation of Artificial Intelligence Technology Used for Ambient Dictation in Primary Care: Comparing the Quality of Documentation of Artificial Intelligence-Generated and Human-Produced Clinical Notes
evidence.outcome: Variation in note quality across competing vendor AI scribe products
evidence.effect: 11 vendor AI scribe tools were compared side by side on standardized cases; all scored below human notes, with wide CIs (e.g., AI 20.3 [15.4 to 25.2] in back pain case).
evidence.quote: Prior evaluations have been vendor specific and not focused on measures of documentation quality.
evidence.sample_unit: AI scribe tools (notes rated by 30 blinded raters across 5 standardized cases, compared with 18 human note takers)

commentary.bottom_line: Two randomized head-to-head trials and several smaller local comparisons found that ambient scribe products differed on documentation time, satisfaction, and note errors, which suggests side-by-side pilots can surface differences that a single-product pilot would miss. No study tested whether choosing a product through such a pilot leads to better outcomes than choosing without one, and vendor rankings shifted with the measurement method used.

perspectives.view: Two randomized trials compared products directly. One found Nabla reduced time-in-note by 7.8% versus DAX, and the other found Product B reduced minutes-in-notes by 3.19 more than Product A. Both show that pilots detect differences, which is an indirect outcome. Small samples, order effects, and method-dependent rankings lower certainty further.

Error audits of identical recordings found 3 errors for one vendor and 8 and 9 for the others, yet Likert ratings ranked a different vendor first. One product had fewer omissions but more irrelevant or misplaced text. Pilots that rely on clinician ratings alone may miss error patterns, so error audits may need to be part of the comparison.

In an 18-physician crossover, DAX was favored on unadjusted burden, note quality, and satisfaction, but adjusted models showed order effects and no overall preference. A 97-clinician pilot found higher utilization for one vendor. These results suggest pilot design, including randomized order and adequate sample size, shapes which product appears better.

One system narrowed 4 vendors to 2 and then 1 through simulations and workflow demonstrations, and it reported reduced vendor influence in selection, but it measured no comparative outcome. None of the studies reported the cost or staff time of running parallel pilots. Leaders may need to budget for these without published estimates.

In one emergency department study, AI scribe notes were similar to or lower in quality than human scribe notes, and in a standardized comparison all 11 AI tools scored below human notes. Patients depend on accurate notes, and these findings suggest the product chosen, and whether it is compared at all, may affect what enters the record.

No comparison study reported enrolling Medicaid, safety-net, limited English proficiency, or low-literacy patients, and none reported whether product rankings held across languages or patient groups. A product that performs better in an academic English-speaking clinic may not perform better with interpreted or multilingual visits.

commentary.research_gap: No study compared outcomes after pilot-based selection with outcomes after selection by other means, such as vendor demonstrations or reference checks. Trials are needed that measure downstream note accuracy, patient harm, and sustained use after selection, and that report the cost of running parallel pilots. Studies should also test whether rankings stay stable across specialties, measurement methods, and patient language groups.
commentary.underserved_note: None of the nine tests reported including Medicaid, safety-net, limited English proficiency, or low-literacy populations, and one did not report its country. Health systems serving these populations cannot assume that a product ranked higher in these pilots will rank higher in their own settings, so their local pilots may need to include encounters with interpreters and multilingual patients.
